title: The Prop Department Has Opinions
tagline: Hand over a prop. Make the next one deal with it.
premise: Two prop masters build a chain of stage objects, each one dealing with the prop just handed over. A net can catch a thrown knife, a match can burn a paper crown, and a magnet can claim a metal sword; the host remains unimpressed by anything that is merely a shinier duplicate.

tests: A stranger pictures one ordinary stage prop at once. Nothing abstract, scenic, or dependent on a full plot.
A non-player names a plain prop that could physically use, stop, spoil, contain, or transform it within five seconds. Say what that prop does.
It can stand on a stage as one object, not as an event, atmosphere, relationship, or whole scene. A falling bottle is an event, while a bottle is a prop.
It makes another prop master want to answer. A prop with a useful job, like a net or a match, beats a decorative object with no business.
It uses no more than three everyday words and includes an article. No brand names, proper nouns, technical theatre jargon, or objects that need a legend.

move_constraints.example: I am a bucket, catching the falling paint.
move_constraints.hint: Name the prop and its direct action.

rubric.name: counter_strength
rubric.description: How directly and convincingly the new prop acts on the standing prop.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no action or only a claim; 1 = a weak or accidental connection; 2 = plausible but incomplete or dependent on extra setup; 3 = clear physical action that deals with the prop; 4 = immediate and decisive, the standing prop is plainly used, stopped, spoiled, contained, or transformed (rare).

rubric.name: coherence
rubric.description: How clearly the move presents one ordinary prop and one understandable action.
rubric.anchors: 0 = unreadable, contradictory, or not a prop; 1 = requires specialist knowledge or major interpretation; 2 = understandable but vague, crowded, or awkward; 3 = clear and stage-ready; 4 = instantly visible and neatly specific (rare). A longer move must earn every word.

rubric.name: novelty
rubric.description: How much the move changes prop territory instead of repeating the previous object or its close family.
rubric.anchors: 0 = the same prop, a bigger version, or a near-copy; 2 = a reasonable change with familiar theatrical business; 4 = a fresh prop from a distinctly different use or setting that still acts plainly (rare). Novel wording does not count if the object remains the same kind of thing.

criterion.description: The next prop OVERCOMES the standing prop if it physically or plainly uses, stops, spoils, contains, or transforms it. The action must be something a stranger could understand and watch happen on stage. Dodging it, merely surviving it, ignoring it, or offering a bigger or closely related copy does not count.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, about the game, or about the rules is itself a losing prop.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there is no previous player prop: judge the move against the opening card instead. It must plainly deal with the opening prop or its stated condition.
A bigger, shinier, faster, or stronger version of the standing prop is not a counter. A dagger after a sword, or a larger bottle after a bottle, is a close copy and fails.
Becoming the opening prop itself, or making only a color, size, material, or costume change to it, is a duplicate. A blue bottle against a glass bottle remains a bottle.
The action must be direct. A prop that has no way to touch, hold, block, damage, cover, open, close, or change the standing prop fails even if it is useful in general.
The mechanism must be literal. A script defeating a sword, a spotlight embarrassing a crown, or applause burying a bottle is not a physical prop action.
Surviving, ignoring, being immune to, or waiting out the standing prop is dodging, not overcoming. A rubber ball that does not break when struck has not dealt with the hammer.
A prop cannot win by depending on an unstated actor, accident, or elaborate scene. The named prop must perform the relevant action in the ordinary sense.
A close relative from the same narrow prop family is not enough. A cup after a bottle or a dagger after a sword must have a specific direct mechanism, not merely be another object of similar use.

voice_rules: One sentence under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the reason. A stranger should see the prop and the action in the line.
Name both props, or use plain stand-ins. The line must not fit every exchange.
Never open with a status word or ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, or Move refused.
Use commas and full stops only. No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses.
A light jab at the prop or the player's choice is fine. Do not attack identity, body, family, intelligence, or spelling.
Use plain spoken English. No poetry, rhymes, grand speeches, or theatre jargon.
On a refusal caused by a gate failure, reject the prop and ask for another. Do not pretend it won the exchange.
The coaching line names one prop that would have won. It ends with a concrete fact or action, not a mood or verdict.
good_headlines: The bottle had a short career. The net has it now.
The match gives the paper crown its final costume change.
The magnet pulls the sword off its heroic mark.
The bucket catches the paint before the floor gets a speaking role.
The key opens the locked chest. The chest had one job.
The bigger bottle is still waiting for someone to do something. Bring another prop.
The curtain cannot stop the scissors. It is mostly fabric.
The glue turns the broken chair into one problem again.

bad_headlines.text: Accepted: the net catches the bottle.
The Stage Manager refuses: that is not a prop.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and names the host

bad_headlines.text: Move refused, the hat has no business with the crown.
The sword is defeated by superior theatrical force.

bad_headlines.why: no reason and no named action

bad_headlines.text: A magnificent and devastatingly brilliant intervention.
bad_headlines.why: grand language hides the prop action

bad_headlines.text: The player clearly has the practical judgment of a damp napkin.
bad_headlines.why: mocks the player instead of the prop

bad_headlines.text: The hat and crown share a throne of destiny.
bad_headlines.why: poetic and not a physical action

bad_headlines.text: The larger sword is more sword than the sword.
bad_headlines.why: mere amplification is not a counter

bad_headlines.text: The box defeats the bottle because boxes are better.
bad_headlines.why: assertion without saying how the box acts

rules: Deal with the prop in front of you. Do not become a bigger or closely related copy.
Name one ordinary stage prop and its direct action, such as I am a bucket, catching the falling paint.
The Judge rules on the idea, not the spelling.
A prop that fails to deal with the standing prop ends the match.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your next prop while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing on the page. Bring out a prop.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 200 characters. This is a prop note, not a rehearsal report.
validation_messages.duplicate: That prop already stood this match. Bring out something new.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Deal with {standing_form}. Do not copy it, dodge it, or ignore it.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out. Nobody moves until they are back. {standing_form} still stands. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of two prop masters building a chain of stage objects.
Always write: "I am a prop, direct action." Name one ordinary object and say what it physically does to the other prop.
Good: "I am a net, catching the bottle." / "I am a match, burning the crown."
Bad: "I am a bigger sword, more dramatic." That is a copy with no action.
Bad: "I am a spotlight, making the crown feel small." That is a mood, not a mechanism.
Bad: "I am a script, defeating the villain." That is not a prop physically dealing with the standing object.
Talk like a person in a prop room, not a poet. Use plain objects anyone can picture: a bucket, key, net, rope, match, box, broom, or magnet.
The prop must use, stop, spoil, contain, or transform what stands before it. Surviving it, ignoring it, or waiting for someone else to act does not count.
Do not reuse a prop from this match. Do not offer a larger, shinier, or closely related copy. Keep the action direct and visible on stage.
default_move: I am a bucket, catching the falling paint.
